mainTopic: Fines for selling animals and slaves to a גוי, and how much gentile partnership exempts an animal from בכורה
overview: This amud first finishes the attempt to prove that a Jew may not sell an animal's future offspring to a גוי. The proof is rejected, because the ברייתא is about a fetus that already exists, as the masculine word בדמיו shows. The גמרא then discusses the קנס for selling a בהמה גסה to a גוי. In one version ריש לקיש says the fine is up to ten times the value. In another version he says up to one hundred, and the גמרא compares this with רבי יהושע בן לוי's fine for selling an עבד. Next the גמרא returns to an animal owned jointly with a גוי. רבי יהודה and חכמים both learn their views from the words ״כל בכור״, and the גמרא gives two ways to explain how each side reads them. רב הונא says even a share in the ear exempts the animal. רב חסדא and רבא say the share must be in a vital part, and their dispute depends on whether a טריפה can live. רב פפא rules that a share in the animal and a share in its mother are treated the same. The amud ends as רבי אלעזר asks רבי אסי what was taught in the בית מדרש, and the answer continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Suggesting the ברייתא refers to the mother animal
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that the ברייתא's ban speaks about the mother animal itself, which would prove that selling rights to future offspring is forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: Isn't the ברייתא talking about the animal itself?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא proposes reading the ברייתא as talking about the mother animal. This would be a proof that one may not give a גוי rights to future offspring.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Suppose the ban is on handing over a non-pregnant animal in exchange for a share of its future offspring. Then giving the גוי a share of future fetuses is already forbidden. Giving him all of the future fetuses would surely be forbidden too. The phrase מאי לאו signals a suggested proof that the גמרא may still knock down.

keyTerms.meaning: What, is it not...? (introduces a suggested reading used as a proof)
An animal; here, the mother animal
Receivership: giving an animal to someone to raise in exchange for a share of the profits or offspring

phrases.english: What, is it not referring to the animal?
phrases.notes: Refers back to the ברייתא quoted on the previous amud.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the proof attempt from the ברייתא cited on the previous amud.
steps.raayaObject: That selling rights to an animal's future offspring to a גוי is forbidden
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא banning giving an animal to a גוי in קבלנות, read as referring to the mother animal

steps.title: No, the ברייתא refers to an existing fetus
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the proof: the ברייתא is about an animal that is already pregnant.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it is talking about a fetus.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes off the proof. The ברייתא speaks about a fetus that already exists inside a pregnant animal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the animal is already pregnant, the ban concerns a real, existing fetus. That tells us nothing about selling rights to future fetuses that do not yet exist. So selling future offspring of a non-pregnant animal to a גוי may still be allowed.

keyTerms.meaning: No: the standard opening of a rejection
A fetus already inside its mother

phrases.english: No, it is referring to a fetus.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the reading proposed in step 1.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the proof from the ברייתא by reinterpreting its case.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof assumed the ברייתא is about the mother animal, but it can be read as being about an existing fetus.

steps.title: The ברייתא's wording backs up the fetus reading
steps.stepSummary: The masculine word בדמיו ('its value') shows the ברייתא is talking about the fetus, not the mother animal.
steps.simpleTranslation: The wording is also exact, because it teaches: 'They fine him up to ten times its value.' Learn from this.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings support for the rejection in step 2 from the exact wording of the ברייתא. It then closes with שמע מינה: 'learn from it.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word בהמה is feminine, so a fine on the mother would say בדמיה. The word עובר is masculine, and the ברייתא says בדמיו in masculine form. So the ברייתא is about the fetus, and the original proof about future offspring falls away.

keyTerms.meaning: The wording is also precise (supports the previous answer)
Learn from it: the point is confirmed

steps.confusionAlert: Do not skip over the small difference between בדמיו (masculine) and בדמיה (feminine). That one letter is the entire proof.

phrases.english: The wording is also precise, for it teaches:
They penalize him up to ten times its value,
phrases.notes: בדמיו is masculine, which fits עובר (fetus) and not בהמה (animal).

phrases.english: Learn from it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the rejection given in step 2.
steps.raayaObject: That the ברייתא refers to an existing fetus
steps.raayaSupportSource: The masculine form בדמיו in the ברייתא
steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא is about a pregnant animal, so it gives no proof that selling future offspring to a גוי is forbidden.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The ברייתא refers to an existing עובר, as the masculine בדמיו shows.

steps.title: The ברייתא supports ריש לקיש's ten-times fine
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא's fine of up to ten times the value supports ריש לקיש, who rules the same fine for selling a בהמה גסה to a גוי.
steps.simpleTranslation: This supports ריש לקיש, for ריש לקיש said: One who sells a large animal to a גוי is fined up to ten times its value.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא notes that the same ברייתא matches a ruling of ריש לקיש. He says that someone who sells a large animal to a גוי is fined up to ten times its value.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Selling a בהמה גסה to a גוי is forbidden by the חכמים. As a penalty, the seller must buy the animal back, even at up to ten times its price. The ברייתא uses the same 'up to ten' measure, so it backs up ריש לקיש.

keyTerms.meaning: Large livestock, such as cows or donkeys
Its value (feminine form, referring to the animal)

phrases.english: This supports Reish Lakish,
for Reish Lakish said:
One who sells large livestock to a gentile —
they penalize him up to ten times its value.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the same ברייתא to support a separate ruling about the size of the קנס.
steps.raayaObject: ריש לקיש's ruling of a fine of up to ten times the value
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא's phrase קונסין אותו עד עשרה
steps.whyThisMatters: It sets the size of the קנס for selling a בהמה גסה to a גוי.

steps.title: Is 'ten times' an exact limit?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether 'up to ten times' is a precise maximum or just a general way of saying 'a lot.'
steps.simpleTranslation: Is it exact, or not exact?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a clarifying question about the number 'ten' in ריש לקיש's ruling. This sets up the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If 'ten' is exact, the fine can never go higher than ten times the value. If it is not exact, it just means a large penalty, and it could be even more.

phrases.english: Is it precise or not precise?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for clarification of the number in step 4.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether 'ten times its value' is a fixed maximum or a loose figure.

steps.title: רבי יהושע בן לוי's fine of up to one hundred for an עבד
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings רבי יהושע בן לוי, who fines one who sells his slave to a גוי up to one hundred times the value. This suggests the number 'ten' is not exact.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: רבי יהושע בן לוי said: One who sells his slave to a גוי is fined up to one hundred times his value!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries to answer the question with a ruling of רבי יהושע בן לוי. He fines someone who sells his slave to a גוי up to one hundred times the value.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If fines can reach one hundred, then the number 'ten' does not seem to be a real limit. The exclamation at the end shows this is meant as a proof that 'ten' is לאו דוקא.

keyTerms.meaning: A non-Jewish slave owned by a Jew, who is obligated in some מצוות

phrases.english: Come and hear,
for Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said:
One who sells his slave to a gentile —
they penalize him up to one hundred times his value!

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע, דְּאָמַר רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן לֵוִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attempts to answer the question of step 5.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי יהושע בן לוי's fine of up to one hundred for selling an עבד

steps.title: A slave is different because he loses מצוות every day
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the comparison: selling an עבד is worse, because each day under the גוי keeps him from doing מצוות.
steps.simpleTranslation: A slave is different, because every single day [the גוי] takes him away from מצוות.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes off the proof. A slave is a special case, so his higher fine teaches nothing about the fine for an animal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An עבד כנעני is obligated in מצוות. Under a גוי owner, he loses them day after day. Because that harm is much greater, the חכמים set a much larger fine of one hundred. This does not show that the 'ten' for an animal is a loose number.

keyTerms.meaning: It is different: introduces a distinction

steps.whatToRemember: The fines are different sizes for a reason: up to ten for a בהמה גסה, and up to one hundred for an עבד, because the עבד loses מצוות every day.

phrases.english: A slave is different,
for each and every day
he removes him from מצוות.
phrases.notes: The גוי owner keeps the slave from performing מצוות.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof brought in step 6.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the comparison between the עבד case and the בהמה case.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The עבד case has a special, ongoing harm (losing מצוות daily), so its larger fine cannot teach about the fine for an animal.

steps.title: Second version: ריש לקיש fines up to one hundred times
steps.stepSummary: A second version of ריש לקיש's ruling: one who sells a בהמה גסה to a גוי is fined up to one hundred times its value.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say a different version: ריש לקיש said that one who sells a large animal to a גוי is fined up to one hundred times its value.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now gives a second report (איכא דאמרי) of what ריש לקיש said. In this version the fine is one hundred times the value instead of ten.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first version, ריש לקיש's fine was ten times, and a ברייתא supported him. In this version his number is much higher, one hundred. This sets up a new problem, because now the ברייתא's 'ten' no longer matches him.

keyTerms.meaning: A large animal, such as a cow or a donkey
They fine or penalize (a rabbinic penalty)

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two versions. In the first version ריש לקיש said ten and the ברייתא supported him. In this version he says one hundred, so the same ברייתא becomes a difficulty.

phrases.english: And there are those who say:
Reish Lakish said:
One who sells a large animal to a gentile
they penalize him
phrases.notes: He must buy it back, even at a high price.

phrases.english: up to one hundred times its value.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a second version of the discussion that began with ריש לקיש's ruling in Step 4.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Selling a בהמה גסה to a גוי is penalized with a buy-back of up to one hundred times its value.

steps.title: The ברייתא says only ten for receivership
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא fines one who gives an animal to a גוי in קבלנות only up to ten times, which seems to contradict ריש לקיש's one hundred.
steps.simpleTranslation: We learned: one who gives a גוי an animal in receivership, even though he is not allowed to, is fined up to ten times its value. This contradicts ריש לקיש!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges ריש לקיש from the ברייתא, which gives only ten times as the fine.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both cases involve placing an animal in a גוי's hands. So why would ריש לקיש fine one hundred when the ברייתא fines only ten? The challenge assumes the two cases should carry the same penalty.

keyTerms.meaning: Receivership: giving an animal to someone to raise in exchange for a share of the profits

phrases.english: We learned:
And one who gives it to him in receivership,
even though he is not permitted to do so,
they penalize him
up to ten times its value!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the ruling just quoted in Step 8.
steps.kashyaTarget: ריש לקיש's fine of one hundred times for selling a בהמה גסה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא sets the fine for a similar case at only ten, so one hundred seems wrong.

steps.title: A sale cuts the animal off completely, receivership does not
steps.stepSummary: Selling removes the animal from the Jew entirely, so the fine is larger. Receivership leaves the animal still his, so the fine is smaller.
steps.simpleTranslation: With a sale, the animal is cut off from him. With receivership, it is not cut off from him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the two cases are different, so their fines can be different.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When he sells, the Jew loses all ownership, and the animal is fully in the גוי's hands. In קבלנות the Jew still owns the animal, so the problem is less severe. That is why the fine is only ten.

keyTerms.meaning: It is cut off or separated from him

phrases.english: A sale: it is cut off from him;
receivership: it is not cut off from him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the contradiction raised in Step 9.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Sale and receivership deserve the same fine.
steps.terutzMaskana: A sale is more severe because ownership is fully transferred, so it gets one hundred, while receivership gets ten.

steps.title: Is 'one hundred' an exact maximum?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether 'up to one hundred' is a precise number or just a way of saying 'a very large amount.'
steps.simpleTranslation: Is it exact, or not exact?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks whether ריש לקיש's number, one hundred, is meant exactly.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the same question asked in the first version about 'ten,' now applied to 'one hundred.' If it is not exact, the fine could go even higher.

phrases.english: Is it exact, or not exact?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Now that ריש לקיש is defended, the גמרא asks how to read his number.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether 'one hundred' is a fixed maximum or an expression meaning 'a great deal.'

steps.title: רבי יהושע בן לוי fines the seller of a slave only ten
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע בן לוי fines one who sells his slave to a גוי up to ten times. This suggests one hundred cannot be an exact required amount.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come hear: רבי יהושע בן לוי said that one who sells his slave to a גוי is fined up to ten times his value!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries to answer the question with a proof from רבי יהושע בן לוי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Selling an עבד to a גוי seems at least as bad as selling an animal, since the slave loses מצוות. Yet רבי יהושע בן לוי gives only ten. This suggests ריש לקיש's 'one hundred' is not a precise number. (In the first version, רבי יהושע בן לוי said one hundred; here he says ten.)

phrases.english: Come and hear:
as Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said:
One who sells his slave to a gentile
they penalize him
up to ten times his value!

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע, דְּאָמַר רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן לֵוִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a source to answer the question in Step 11.
steps.raayaObject: That 'one hundred' is not an exact figure
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי יהושע בן לוי's ruling of ten times for selling a slave to a גוי

steps.title: A slave is different: he does not come back
steps.stepSummary: The proof is rejected. A slave who is bought back goes free and does not return to his owner, so the owner already suffers a loss and is fined less.
steps.simpleTranslation: A slave is different, because he does not come back to him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the proof by showing that a slave is a different case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When the owner redeems a slave from a גוי, the slave goes free rather than returning to him. Since the owner loses the slave anyway, חז"ל gave a smaller fine. An animal, by contrast, comes back to its owner.

phrases.english: A slave is different,
since he does not return to him.
phrases.notes: Once redeemed, the slave goes free.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof brought in Step 12.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The comparison between slave and animal
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The slave's owner loses the slave even after redeeming him, so his fine is reduced.

steps.title: Then the animal should cost only one more
steps.stepSummary: If an animal is fined more only because it comes back to the owner, the extra fine should be just one unit (eleven), not ninety more.
steps.simpleTranslation: Why is the fine for an animal higher? Because it comes back to him? Then fine him just one more!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the rejection from Step 13.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The difference between the slave and the animal is only that the animal returns, which is worth about one unit of its value. That could explain eleven, but not a jump from ten to one hundred. So 'he does not return' cannot explain the gap.

phrases.english: An animal: what is the reason it is fined more?
Because it returns to him?
Then penalize him only one more!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the rejection given in Step 13.
steps.kashyaTarget: The distinction that a slave does not return while an animal does
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The distinction is too small to explain the gap between ten and one hundred; it would justify only eleven.

steps.title: Selling a slave is rare, so חז"ל did not fully decree
steps.stepSummary: A new distinction: selling a slave to a גוי is uncommon, and חז"ל do not make decrees for uncommon situations, so the slave case cannot teach about the animal case.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather: a slave is something uncommon, and for anything uncommon the רבנן did not make a decree.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא drops the 'does not return' answer and gives a new reason why the slave case cannot be compared to the animal case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Selling an animal to a גוי happens often, so חז"ל made a strong penalty. Selling a slave is rare, so they did not put their full penalty on it. Since the slave fine is not a full decree, it proves nothing about the number one hundred, and the question remains open.

keyTerms.meaning: The רבנן did not make a decree for it

steps.whatToRemember: In this version ריש לקיש fines one hundred for selling a בהמה גסה. That is larger than receivership (ten), because a sale fully transfers ownership. רבי יהושע בן לוי's ten for a slave does not disprove one hundred, because selling a slave is rare and חז"ל do not decree for rare cases.
steps.whyThisMatters: The rule 'מילתא דלא שכיחא לא גזרו בה רבנן' is a general principle across ש"ס: rabbinic decrees target common situations.

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא, עֶבֶד — מִילְּתָא דְלָא שְׁכִיחָא הִיא,
phrases.english: Rather, a slave is an uncommon matter,
and any uncommon matter,
the Rabbis did not decree regarding it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא, עֶבֶד — מִילְּתָא דְלָא שְׁכִיחָא הִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 14 by replacing Step 13's distinction with a new one, which again rejects the proof of Step 12.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The slave is fined less because he does not return to the owner.
steps.terutzMaskana: The slave is fined less because selling a slave is rare, and חז"ל do not make full decrees for rare cases.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The slave case cannot be used to prove that 'one hundred' is not exact.

steps.title: Both sides learn from the same verse
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings back the view of חכמים from the ברייתא. רבי יהושע says that both חכמים and רבי יהודה learn their view from the same words, ״כל בכור״.
steps.simpleTranslation: And חכמים say: as long as the גוי has a hand in it, etc. רבי יהושע said: Both of them learned from one פסוק, ״כל בכור״.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא returns to the ברייתא and quotes the view of חכמים. Then רבי יהושע says both opinions come from the same פסוק. This sets up the next step, which explains how each side reads it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהודה says the Jew's share of a jointly owned animal is a בכור. חכמים say that any ownership by a גוי exempts the animal. רבי יהושע tells us this is not a debate about different sources. It is a debate about how to read the same two words, ״כל בכור״.

keyTerms.meaning: The gentile's 'hand,' meaning his ownership or share

phrases.english: And the Sages say:
As long as the gentile has a hand (ownership) in it, etc.
phrases.notes: A short quote of the ברייתא from 2b. The full ruling is that such an animal is exempt from בכורה.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehoshua said:
And both of them learned from one verse,
'All the firstborn.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the side discussion about fines for selling to a גוי and returns to the ברייתא about animals jointly owned with a גוי.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Both רבי יהודה and חכמים learn their rulings on a partly gentile-owned animal from the words ״כל בכור״.

steps.title: How each side reads the word 'all'
steps.stepSummary: חכמים say 'בכור' alone would include even a partial בכור, so 'כל' requires the whole animal. רבי יהודה says 'בכור' alone would mean only a fully owned בכור, so 'כל' includes even a small share.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבנן hold: 'בכור' alone means even part of a בכור. The תורה wrote 'כל' to require the whole animal. רבי יהודה holds: 'בכור' alone means a whole בכור. The תורה wrote 'כל' to include even any amount.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains exactly how each side uses the same words. They disagree about what the word בכור would mean without the word כל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both sides agree that the word כל changes the meaning. They disagree about the starting point. For חכמים, plain 'בכור' would be broad, so כל narrows it to the whole animal. For רבי יהודה, plain 'בכור' would be narrow, so כל widens it to include even a partial share.

keyTerms.meaning: Any amount at all, even a tiny bit

steps.confusionAlert: Both sides use the same word, כל, but it moves in opposite directions. For חכמים it makes the rule stricter about ownership (the whole animal must be Jewish-owned). For רבי יהודה it makes the rule wider (even a small Jewish share counts). Keep track of which side each one starts from.

phrases.english: The Rabbis hold:
'Firstborn' implies even part of a firstborn,
So the Merciful One wrote 'all' —
Meaning not until the whole of it is there (Jewish-owned).
And Rabbi Yehuda holds:
'Firstborn' implies the whole firstborn,
So the Merciful One wrote 'all' —
Meaning even any amount at all.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Spells out the claim of רבי יהושע by showing how each side reads ״כל בכור״.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: חכמים: 'כל' requires full Jewish ownership. רבי יהודה: 'כל' includes even partial Jewish ownership.

steps.title: A second explanation: both agree on 'majority'
steps.stepSummary: Another approach: everyone agrees that plain 'בכור' means mostly Jewish-owned. The debate is whether 'כל' adds to that (requiring the whole animal) or takes away from it (including even a minority share).
steps.simpleTranslation: If you want, say instead: everyone agrees 'firstborn' means the majority. One Sage holds 'all' comes to fill it up (require the whole). The other Sage holds it comes to reduce (include even less).
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers a different way to explain the same debate. This time both sides start from the same meaning of the word בכור.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this version, both sides agree on what בכור means by itself: a majority share. They argue only about what כל does. חכמים say it adds, so the whole animal must be Jewish-owned. רבי יהודה says it takes away, so even a minority share is enough.

keyTerms.meaning: If you wish, say (introduces an alternative explanation)
To fill up / to add (require more)
To reduce / to take away (require less)

steps.whatToRemember: There are two ways to explain the debate over ״כל בכור״. (1) The sides disagree about what 'בכור' means alone, and כל pushes each in the opposite direction. (2) Both agree 'בכור' means a majority, and they disagree whether כל adds (חכמים) or takes away (רבי יהודה).

phrases.english: If you wish, say:
According to everyone, 'firstborn' implies the majority,
One Sage holds: 'all' implies
That it comes to fill up (require the whole),
phrases.notes: This is the view of חכמים.

phrases.english: And the other Sage holds: it comes to reduce (include even a minority).
phrases.notes: This is the view of רבי יהודה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second way to explain the same disagreement explained in step 17.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Both agree that 'בכור' alone means majority ownership. חכמים read כל as adding (the whole animal), and רבי יהודה reads it as reducing (even a minority).

steps.title: How small can the gentile's share be?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how small the גוי's share can be, according to חכמים, and still exempt the animal from בכורה.
steps.simpleTranslation: And how much must the gentile's partnership be for the animal to be exempt from firstborn status?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a practical follow-up question: what is the smallest share the גוי can own and still exempt the animal? The answer comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: חכמים said that any ownership by a גוי exempts the animal. The גמרא now wants to know the minimum. Is even a tiny part, like a single limb, enough?

phrases.english: And how much must the gentile's partnership be,
For the animal to be exempt from firstborn status?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the source of the rule to the exact limits of the rule of חכמים.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The smallest share a גוי can own and still exempt the animal from בכורה.

steps.title: Even owning just the ear is enough
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא answers that even if the גוי owns only the animal's ear, the animal is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא said: Even its ear.
steps.whatsHappening: רב הונא answers the question: a very small share, even just the ear, is enough to exempt the animal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This takes the view of חכמים literally: any gentile ownership exempts the animal. There is no minimum size, and even one ear counts.

phrases.english: Rav Huna said:
Even its ear.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 19.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Even if the גוי owns only the ear, the animal is exempt from בכורה.

steps.title: Why not just give the gentile his ear?
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן challenges רב הונא: why should a share as small as an ear exempt the animal? We could just tell the גוי, 'take your ear and go.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן objected: But let him say to him, 'Take your ear and go!'
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן attacks the answer of רב הונא. If the גוי owns only the ear, his share can easily be separated and handed to him, so the rest of the animal should still be a בכור.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge is that a tiny, separable part should not cancel the holiness of the whole animal. The animal could keep its status as a בכור, and the כהן could tell the גוי, 'take your ear and go.' Cutting off the ear makes the בכור blemished, and a blemished בכור belongs to the כהן anyway.

keyTerms.meaning: He objected to it (a strong challenge)

phrases.english: Rav Nachman objected to this:
But let him (the כהן) say to him (the גוי):
'Take your ear and go!'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of רב הונא in step 20.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling of רב הונא that owning only the ear exempts the animal from בכורה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A share as small as an ear can be cut off and handed to the גוי. So it should not take away the status of בכור from the whole animal.

steps.title: The גוי's share must be in a vital part of the animal
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא says the גוי's share must be in a part whose removal would make the animal a נבלה. רבא says a part whose removal would make it a טריפה is enough.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was stated: רב חסדא said, the גוי must own a part of the animal that, if removed, would make it a נבלה (it would die right away). רבא said, a part that, if removed, would make it a טריפה (it would eventually die).
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a different opinion about how big the גוי's share must be. These אמוראים say a share in the ear is not enough. The share has to be in a part the animal needs to live.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This fits רב נחמן's objection: a tiny, non-vital share like an ear can simply be handed back to the גוי. Both אמוראים require a share in a part the animal's life depends on. They disagree only on how strictly 'life depends on it' is defined. Under רבא, a share in a טריפה-making part already exempts the animal, so more animals are exempt. Under רב חסדא, only a נבלה-making part counts.

keyTerms.meaning: An animal that died without proper שחיטה. Here it means a part whose loss kills the animal immediately.
An animal with a fatal defect. Here it means a part whose loss will make the animal die eventually.
A part that makes it (that is, whose removal makes the animal) a נבלה or a טריפה.

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two opinions. רב חסדא is the stricter one about what counts as a meaningful share (only a נבלה-making part). רבא accepts the broader group of טריפה-making parts.

phrases.english: It was stated: Rav Chisda said:
a part [whose removal] makes it a carcass (nevelah);
and Rava said:
a part [whose removal] makes it a tereifa.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a different answer to the question of step 19, one that avoids רב נחמן's objection to רב הונא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The גוי's share exempts the animal only if it is in a vital part. For רב חסדא that means a נבלה-making part. For רבא it includes a טריפה-making part.

steps.title: What is the root of their disagreement?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what principle רב חסדא and רבא are really arguing about.
steps.simpleTranslation: About what do they disagree?
steps.whatsHappening: This is a setup line. The גמרא asks for the underlying reason behind the dispute, and the next step gives the answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both אמוראים agree that the share must be in a vital part. The question is why they draw the line in different places.

keyTerms.meaning: About what do they disagree? This asks for the root principle of a dispute.

phrases.english: About what do they disagree?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the basis of the dispute stated in step 22.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which principle splits רב חסדא and רבא.

steps.title: Can a טריפה survive?
steps.stepSummary: They disagree about whether a טריפה can live. רבא holds it cannot, so a טריפה-making part is vital. רב חסדא holds it can, so only a נבלה-making part is vital.
steps.simpleTranslation: They disagree about whether a טריפה can live. The one who says 'a part that makes it a טריפה' holds that a טריפה cannot live. The one who says 'a part that makes it a נבלה' holds that a טריפה can live.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers its question. The dispute depends on whether an animal that is a טריפה can go on living.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both opinions say the vital part is one the animal cannot survive without. רבא holds a טריפה cannot survive, so losing a טריפה-making part already counts as losing life. רב חסדא holds a טריפה can survive, so only a part whose loss kills the animal on the spot (נבלה) is truly vital.

keyTerms.meaning: A טריפה can live. This is the debated principle.
According to the one who says.

steps.whyThisMatters: Whether a טריפה can live is a well-known dispute that comes up across ש״ס. Here it decides how much of an animal a גוי must own to block בכורה.

phrases.english: About whether a tereifa can live.

phrases.aramaic: לְמַאן דְּאָמַר דָּבָר שֶׁעוֹשֶׂה אוֹתוֹ טְרֵיפָה —
phrases.english: According to the one who says a part that makes it a tereifa (Rava),
he holds that a tereifa cannot live;

phrases.aramaic: וּלְמַאן דְּאָמַר דָּבָר שֶׁעוֹשֶׂה אוֹתוֹ נְבֵלָה —
phrases.english: and according to the one who says a part that makes it a carcass (Rav Chisda),
but a tereifa can live.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 23.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The dispute depends on whether a טריפה can live: רבא says it cannot, and רב חסדא says it can.

steps.title: A proposal that רב הונא does not argue with רב חסדא and רבא
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים suggest to רב פפא that רב הונא's 'ear' ruling is about a share in the newborn itself, while רב חסדא and רבא are talking about a share in its mother.
steps.simpleTranslation: The חכמים said before רב פפא: רב הונא's ruling and the ruling of רב חסדא and רבא do not disagree. This one is about a share in the animal itself, and that one is about a share in its mother.
steps.whatsHappening: The חכמים try to make peace between the opinions. They suggest each opinion is about a different case, so there is no real argument.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to this suggestion, if the גוי owns even an ear of the firstborn itself, it is not 'all' a בכור, so it is exempt. If the גוי's share is only in the mother, the share must be in a vital part to exempt the offspring. This would remove the conflict between 'an ear is enough' and 'a vital part is needed'.

keyTerms.meaning: The חכמים said it before (a teacher). They are proposing an idea to him.
This one is about it (the animal itself), and that one is about its mother.

steps.confusionAlert: 'בו' means the גוי is a partner in the firstborn animal itself. 'באמו' means the גוי is a partner only in the mother that gave birth to it.

phrases.english: The Sages said it before Rav Pappa:

phrases.aramaic: הָא דְּרַב הוּנָא, וְרַב חִסְדָּא וְרָבָא —
phrases.english: This [ruling] of Rav Huna, and [that of] Rav Chisda and Rava,
do not disagree;
this (Rav Huna) is about [a share in] it, and that (Rav Chisda and Rava) is about [a share in] its mother.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tries to reconcile רב הונא (step 20) with רב חסדא and רבא (step 22).
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (אוקימתא): each opinion is about a different situation.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב הונא and רב חסדא/רבא seem to give conflicting answers to the same question.
steps.terutzMaskana: רב הונא is about a share in the firstborn itself, and רב חסדא/רבא are about a share in its mother.

steps.title: רב פפא: the mother also needs 'כל'
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא rejects the distinction. If a share in the animal itself exempts because the verse says 'כל בכור', the mother is also covered by a verse with 'כל': 'כל מקנך תזכר'.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said to them: What is different about the animal itself? That we need 'all the firstborn' and it is missing? For the mother too we need 'all your livestock shall bear males', and that is missing!
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא pushes back on the חכמים' suggestion. The reason that works for the animal itself works just as well for the mother.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The only reason a tiny share in the animal itself would exempt it is the word 'כל' in 'כל בכור'. But the verse about the mother, 'כל מקנך תזכר', also uses 'כל'. That means the mother must also be fully Jewish-owned. So there is no basis for treating a share in the mother differently.

keyTerms.meaning: And it is not there (the requirement is missing).
'All your livestock that bears males' (שמות לד:יט). This verse speaks about the mother.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said to them:
What is different about [a share in] it,
that we require 'all the firstborn' and it is not there?
For its mother too we require
'all your livestock shall bear males', and it is not there!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לְהוּ רַב פָּפָּא: מַאי שְׁנָא בּוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reconciliation proposed in step 25.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The proposed split between a share in the animal itself and a share in its mother.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The verses for both cases use 'כל', so the reasoning that applies to the animal applies equally to the mother.

steps.title: There is no difference between the two cases
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא concludes that the animal itself and its mother are treated the same, so רב הונא really does argue with רב חסדא and רבא.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, there is no difference.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא wraps up his point. The two cases are the same, so the dispute between the אמוראים stays in place for both.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since 'כל' applies to both the animal and its mother, one rule covers both. רב הונא would say an ear is enough in both cases. רב חסדא and רבא would require a vital part in both cases.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather. This introduces the corrected conclusion.

steps.whatToRemember: How big must a גוי's share be to exempt an animal from בכורה? רב הונא says even an ear is enough. רב חסדא requires a נבלה-making part. רבא requires a טריפה-making part, based on his view that a טריפה cannot live. רב פפא rules that this dispute applies equally to a share in the animal itself and a share in its mother.

phrases.english: Rather, there is no difference.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes רב פפא's rejection with a concluding rule.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: A share in the animal itself and a share in its mother are treated alike, so רב הונא genuinely disagrees with רב חסדא and רבא in both cases.

steps.title: Why should a vital part matter if non-viable newborns are still holy?
steps.stepSummary: מר בר רב אשי asks why a non-Jew's share in a vital part should exempt the animal from בכור status. After all, נפלים, which cannot survive, are still holy as a בכור, based on the verse 'פטר שגר בהמה'.
steps.simpleTranslation: מר בר רב אשי challenged this: How is this different from נפלים (non-viable newborns)? Even though they cannot live, they are holy. As the Master said: 'פטר שגר בהמה' teaches that whatever dwells inside an animal (in its womb) is holy.
steps.whatsHappening: מר בר רב אשי attacks the reasoning we just saw. That reasoning says a non-Jew's share in a part the animal cannot live without exempts it. He asks: why should being able to live matter at all for בכור?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier logic was built on viability. A share in a part the animal needs to live counts like a share in the whole animal. מר בר רב אשי points out that viability is not required for בכור holiness, because even נפלים are holy. So 'it can't live without this part' seems like the wrong test.

keyTerms.meaning: He challenged it (a strong objection to a statement)
Non-viable newborns, born unable to survive
'The firstborn that emerges from an animal' (שמות יג:יב)
Read as 'that which dwells', meaning in the womb

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think מר בר רב אשי is saying a non-Jew's share never matters. He is only attacking the specific idea that viability is what makes a part important for בכור.

phrases.aramaic: מַתְקֵיף לַהּ מָר בַּר רַב אָשֵׁי:
phrases.english: Mar bar Rav Ashi challenged this:
How is this different from non-viable newborns,

phrases.aramaic: דְּאַף עַל גַּב דְּלָאו בְּנֵי חִיּוּתָא נִינְהוּ קָדְשִׁי,
phrases.english: which, even though they are not viable, are holy?
As the Master said: 'the firstborn that emerges from [sheger] an animal'
means: whatever dwells in an animal (its womb) is holy!

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְקֵיף לַהּ מָר בַּר רַב אָשֵׁי: מַאי שְׁנָא מִנְּפָלִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the viability-based reasoning behind the vital-part exemption discussed by רב חסדא and רבא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea that a non-Jew's share in a part the animal cannot live without exempts it from בכור status.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: נפלים are holy as a בכור even though they cannot live. So viability should not decide whether בכור holiness applies.

steps.title: The real issue is a non-holy part mixed in, not viability
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that נפלים have no חולין mixed into them, so 'כל בכור' applies to them. When a non-Jew owns a vital part, חולין is mixed in, so 'כל בכור' does not apply.
steps.simpleTranslation: There (with נפלים), since no חולין is mixed into them, we apply to the animal the phrase 'כל בכור' (all the firstborn). Here, since חולין is mixed in, we do not apply 'כל בכור'.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends the vital-part rule. It explains that the problem is not whether the animal can live. The problem is that the non-Jew's share mixes something non-holy into the animal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A נפל is completely Jewish-owned, so the whole animal can be 'כל בכור', all of it holy. When a non-Jew owns a vital part, that share counts as a share in the whole animal, so חולין is mixed through it. The verse demands 'כל', a complete בכור, so it is exempt. Viability only tells us which parts count as a share in the whole.

keyTerms.meaning: We apply the verse to them

steps.whatToRemember: בכור holiness needs 'כל בכור', a complete, unmixed firstborn. A נפל qualifies even though it cannot live. An animal with a non-Jew's share in a vital part does not qualify, because חולין is mixed in.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shifts the test from 'can it live?' to 'is any non-holy ownership mixed in?' That keeps the exemption rule from the earlier steps standing.

phrases.aramaic: הָתָם, כֵּיוָן דְּלָא עָרִיבוּ בְּהוּ חוּלִּין —
phrases.english: There, since no non-holy element is mixed into them,
we apply to the animal the phrase 'all the firstborn'.
Here, since a non-holy element is mixed in,
we do not apply to them 'all the firstborn'.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָתָם, כֵּיוָן דְּלָא עָרִיבוּ בְּהוּ חוּלִּין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers מר בר רב אשי's challenge by pointing to a difference between נפלים and our case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the cases (חילוק): mixed ownership versus no mixture
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Viability decides בכור status, so נפלים should be no different from a vital-part case.
steps.terutzMaskana: The deciding factor is whether חולין is mixed in. Without a mixture, 'כל בכור' applies. With a non-Jew's share in a vital part, it does not.

steps.title: רבי אלעזר asks רבי אסי what was taught in the study hall
steps.stepSummary: A new story begins. רבי אלעזר did not go into the בית מדרש. He met רבי אסי and asked him what the חכמים said there. רבי אסי begins to answer.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר did not enter the בית מדרש. He found רבי אסי and said to him: What did the חכמים say in the בית מדרש? He said to him:
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up the next move. It opens a short story where רבי אלעזר asks what he missed in the בית מדרש. רבי אסי's answer comes in the next part of the text.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Nothing is ruled yet. This step only frames a new teaching that will be reported in רבי אסי's name. The words 'אמר ליה' at the end tell us his answer is about to be quoted.

keyTerms.meaning: He found him, he met him

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר לָא עַל לְבֵי מִדְרְשָׁא,
phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar did not enter the study hall.
He found Rabbi Asi,

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: מַאי אֲמוּר רַבָּנַן בֵּי מִדְרְשָׁא?
phrases.english: and said to him: What did the Sages say in the study hall?
He said to him:

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר לָא עַל לְבֵי מִדְרְשָׁא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new section after the previous discussion was resolved.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the חכמים taught in the בית מדרש while רבי אלעזר was absent.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Not yet given. רבי אסי's answer begins on the next amud.
